ety.text: From Middle English yvel, evel, ivel, uvel, from Old English yfel, from Proto-West Germanic *ubil, from Proto-Germanic *ubilaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂up(h₁)élos, a deverbal derivative of *h₂wep(h₁)-, *h₂wop(h₁)- (“treat badly”). See -le for the supposed suffix. Alternatively from *upélos (“evil”, literally “going over or beyond (acceptable limits)”), from Proto-Indo-European *upo, *h₃ewp- (“down, up, over”).

From Middle English yvele, yvel, ivel, from Old English yfele (“badly, evilly”), a derivative of the adjective yfel (“bad, evil”). Often reinterpreted as the noun in the later language (as in "to speak evil").

senses.d: Intending to harm; malevolent.
ex: an evil plot to brainwash and even kill innocent people
For a good while the Miss Brownings were kept in ignorance of the evil tongues that whispered hard words about Molly.

senses.d: Morally corrupt.
ex: If something is evil, it is never mandatory.
Do you think that companies that engage in animal testing are evil?

senses.d: Unpleasant, foul (of odor, taste, mood, weather, etc.).
ex: He awoke in an evil temper […]
He herded them into a small and evil toilet and then through a window.

senses.d: Producing or threatening sorrow, distress, injury, or calamity; unpropitious; calamitous.
ex: The owl shrieked at thy birth,—an evil sign;
[…] he hath brought up an evil name upon a virgin of Israel:

senses.d: Having harmful qualities; not good; worthless or deleterious.
ex: an evil beast; an evil plant; an evil crop
A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit.

senses.d: Undesirable; harmful; bad practice.
ex: Global variables are evil; storing processing context in object member variables allows those objects to be reused in a much more flexible way.

senses.d: Moral badness; wickedness; malevolence; the forces or behaviors that are the opposite or enemy of good.
ex: The evils of society include murder and theft.
Evil lacks spirituality, hence its need for mind control.

senses.d: Something which impairs the happiness of a being or deprives a being of any good; something which causes suffering of any kind to sentient beings; harm; injury; mischief.
ex: evils which our own misdeeds have wrought
The evil that men do lives after them.

senses.d: A malady or disease; especially in combination, as in king's evil, colt evil.
ex: [The disease]Tis call'd the Euill.
He [Edward the Confessor] was the first that touched for the evil.

senses.d: wickedly, evilly, iniquitously
ex: O what of Gods then boots it to be borne, / If old Aveugles ſonnes ſo euill heare?

senses.d: injuriously, harmfully; in a damaging way.
ex: And many ſhall follow their pernicious wayes, by reaſon of whom the way of trueth ſhall be euill ſpoken of:

senses.d: badly, poorly; in an insufficient way.
ex: It went evil with him.

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French maulvais, from Old French malvais, malveis (“evil, wicked, bad, of poor or inferior quality", later also "unlucky”), from Late Latin malifātius (“unfortunate”, 4th c.), from Latin malus (“bad”) + fātum (“fate”).
Borrowed from Latin maleficus.

From Middle French meschant (“bad; wrong”), from Old French mescheant (“hapless, unlucky; worthless”), from mescheoir (“to misfall, happen unfavourably”); equivalent to mé- + choir. For sense evolution, compare mauvais.
Borrowed from Old Occitan malvatz, from Late Latin malifātius (“unfortunate”). Cognate with Spanish and Portuguese malvado, and more distantly with French mauvais.
From Latin malevolus.
From Latin malignus.
Inherited from Old Spanish malo, from Latin malus. Cognate with Ladino malo, Italian malo, Galician mao, Portuguese mau.
Borrowed from Old Occitan malvat, from Late Latin malifātius (“unfortunate”).
From Latin malevolus.
Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese mao, from Latin malus, from Proto-Italic. Cognate with Galician mao and Spanish malo.
Borrowed from Latin maleficus, from male (“badly, evilly”) + facio (“do”).
From Spanish malvado, from Old Occitan malvat, from Late Latin malifātius (“unfortunate”).
From mal- + faisant.
Inherited from Latin captīvus (“captive” → “caught by the devil” → “bad”). Compare the semantic development of French chétif (“puny, scrawny”) and Galician cativo.

ety.text: From Middle English evidence, from Old French [Term?], from Latin evidentia (“clearness, in Late Latin a proof”), from evidens (“clear, evident”); see evident.

senses.d: Facts or observations presented in support of an assertion.
ex: There is no demonstrative evidence that anyone was here earlier.
We have enough cold hard evidence in that presentation which will make a world of pain for our parasitic friends at Antarctica.

senses.d: Anything admitted by a court to prove or disprove alleged matters of fact in a trial.
One who bears witness.
ex: infamous and perjured evidences

senses.d: A body of objectively verifiable facts that are positively indicative of, and/or exclusively concordant with, that one conclusion over any other.
To provide evidence for, or suggest the truth of.
ex: She was furious, as evidenced by her slamming the door.

grp.label: facts or observations presented in support of an assertion
anything admitted by a court as proof

ety.text: From Middle French preuve, from Old French prueve, preuve; synchronically derivable from the verb prouver. Possibly corresponds to Late Latin proba, from Latin probō.
Either deverbal from provare (“to try; to test; to prove; to feel”) + -a, or from Late Latin proba, from Latin probō.

From Middle English evident, from Old French evident, from Latin ēvidēns (“visible, apparent, clear, plain”) (compare Late Latin ēvideor (“to appear plainly”)), from ē (“out”) + videō (“see”), present participle vidēns, deponent videor (“to appear, seem”). Displaced native Old English sweotol.

senses.d: Obviously true by simple observation.
ex: It was evident she was angry, after she slammed the door.
The full extent of her injuries did not become evident until they tried to move her.
